```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
library(bayescompR)
```

`vignette("inference")` covers NUTS, the other kernels of
`bayescomp_sample()`, optimization, ADVI, Pathfinder and tempered SMC. This
vignette covers the rest: samplers for multimodal posteriors, gradient free
ensembles, Gibbs sampling, samplers that adapt to local geometry, piecewise
deterministic processes, state space models, large data methods, model
comparison and simulation based inference. Every function returns a
`bayescomp_fit`, so `summary()`, `bayescomp_extract()`, the diagnostics and
`plot()` work the same way. The runs below are short to keep the vignette
quick; real analyses need longer ones.

Each section names what the method needs from the model and whether its
draws are exact (the Markov chain leaves the posterior invariant) or
approximate.

## A multimodal target

Two well separated modes trap NUTS in whichever mode it starts in.

```{r}
mix <- bayescomp_model("
  parameters { real x; }
  model { target += log_mix(0.3, normal_lpdf(x | -5, 0.5), normal_lpdf(x | 5, 0.5)); }
")
```

### Parallel tempering

`bayescomp_parallel_tempering()` runs replicas of the bridge
$g^{1 - \beta} p^\beta$ between a Gaussian reference `g` and the
posterior `p`, lets neighbors swap states, and keeps the $\beta = 1$
replica. Swaps are non reversible by default (Syed et al. 2022): even and
odd pairs alternate, so states travel along the ladder in persistent sweeps.
During warmup the temperatures move so that every pair rejects swaps at the
same rate. Needs: log density. Exact.

```{r}
pt <- bayescomp_parallel_tempering(mix, num_temps = 8, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 300,
                                   iter_sampling = 600, reference = "standard",
                                   reference_scale = 8, seed = 1)
mean(bayescomp_extract(pt, "x") < 0)
round(pt$betas[[1]], 3)
round(pt$swap_rate[[1]], 2)
pt$log_evidence
```

The share of draws in the left mode is near its weight 0.3. The stepping
stone evidence estimate is near 0, the log normalizing constant of this
density. `barrier` is the estimated global communication barrier
$\Lambda$; the schedule needs about $2 \Lambda$ temperatures.

### Reverse diffusion Monte Carlo

`bayescomp_diffusion()` (experimental) follows the time reversal of an
Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process from a standard normal to the target, with the
score estimated by importance sampling at every step (Huang et al. 2024).
Its draws are independent and move between modes without a Markov chain,
but they are approximate.

```{r}
dm <- bayescomp_diffusion(mix, num_samples = 150, steps = 30, inner_samples = 24,
                          reference = "standard", reference_scale = 5, seed = 1)
mean(bayescomp_extract(dm, "x") < 0)
```

## Gradient free samplers

```{r}
corr <- bayescomp_model("
  parameters { vector[2] x; real<lower=0> s; }
  model {
    x ~ multi_normal([1, -1]', [[1, 0.9], [0.9, 1]]);
    s ~ gamma(3, 2);
  }
")
```

### Elliptical slice sampling

`algorithm = "elliptical_slice"` writes the posterior as a Gaussian times a
remainder and runs elliptical slice sampling on the remainder (Nishihara
et al. 2014). The Gaussian is fitted during a slice sampling warmup, so the
sampler has no step size. Needs: log density. Exact.

```{r}
es <- bayescomp_sample(corr, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 300, iter_sampling = 500,
                       algorithm = "elliptical_slice", metric = "dense_e", seed = 1, refresh = 0)
summary(es)
```

### Ensemble samplers

`bayescomp_ensemble()` moves a population of walkers, each using the
others to propose: the affine invariant stretch move (Goodman and Weare
2010) or differential evolution (ter Braak 2006). Both are invariant to
linear transformations of the parameters. Walkers are reported as chains;
they are not independent, so R-hat across walkers is optimistic. Needs: log
density. Exact.

```{r}
de <- bayescomp_ensemble(corr, method = "de", iter_warmup = 300, iter_sampling = 300, seed = 1)
summary(de)[, c("variable", "mean", "sd")]
mean(de$acceptance)
```

## Gibbs sampling

`bayescomp_gibbs()` updates one block of parameters at a time. With
`kernel = "auto"` it tests whether each block's full conditional is
Gaussian (log density quadratic), Gamma (positive scalar with log density
$a \log x - b x^k$) or Beta (unit interval scalar), by fitting the family
at several random states and checking its predictions. A detected block is
drawn exactly from its conditional; the others use slice sampling. During
warmup each draw is an independence Metropolis step whose acceptance is one
when the detection is right, so a wrong detection shows up as acceptance
below one; blocks accepted every time are drawn directly after warmup.
Needs: log density. Exact when the detection is right.

```{r}
y <- c(1, 2, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5)
nm <- bayescomp_model("
  data { int N; vector[N] y; }
  parameters { real mu; real<lower=0> tau; real<lower=0> nu; }
  model {
    mu ~ normal(0, 10);
    tau ~ gamma(2, 1);
    nu ~ lognormal(0, 1);
    y ~ normal(mu, inv_sqrt(tau));
  }
", data = list(N = 5, y = y))
gb <- bayescomp_gibbs(nm, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 200, iter_sampling = 500, seed = 1)
gb$blocks
```

All three blocks are detected: `nu` has a lognormal prior and does not
enter the likelihood, so its conditional on the unconstrained scale
`log(nu)` is Gaussian.

Blocks and kernels can be chosen by hand, for example random walk
Metropolis on a pair of correlated parameters and MALA on the rest:

```{r}
gb2 <- bayescomp_gibbs(nm, blocks = list(list(pars = c("mu", "tau"), kernel = "metropolis"),
                                         list(pars = "nu", kernel = "mala")),
                       chains = 2, iter_warmup = 300, iter_sampling = 500, seed = 1)
gb2$blocks
```

## Local geometry

`bayescomp_riemannian()` uses a position dependent metric, the SoftAbs
transform of the Hessian (Betancourt 2013). `"smmala"` (simplified
manifold MALA) is exact; `"rmhmc"` integrates with the implicit generalized
leapfrog. Hessians come from finite differences of gradients, so the cost
grows with the square of the dimension: these are for small, strongly
curved models. Needs: gradient.

`bayescomp_mclmc()` is microcanonical Langevin Monte Carlo (Robnik et al.
2023): unit speed dynamics with partial velocity refreshment and no
accept step. It is fast per gradient but approximate.

```{r}
sm <- bayescomp_riemannian(corr, "smmala", chains = 2, iter_warmup = 150, iter_sampling = 300, seed = 1)
mc <- bayescomp_mclmc(corr, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 500, iter_sampling = 1000, seed = 1)
rbind(smmala = summary(sm)$mean[2:4], mclmc = summary(mc)$mean[2:4])
```

## Piecewise deterministic samplers

`bayescomp_pdmp()` runs the Zig-Zag sampler (Bierkens et al. 2019) or the
bouncy particle sampler (Bouchard-Cote et al. 2018): the state moves in
straight lines and the velocity flips or reflects at random event times
driven by the gradient. The event times are found by integrating the rate
numerically, so the draws are approximate with error set by `dt`. Needs:
gradient.

```{r}
zz <- bayescomp_pdmp(corr, "zigzag", chains = 2, iter_warmup = 150, iter_sampling = 400, seed = 1)
summary(zz)[, c("variable", "mean", "sd", "ess_bulk")]
```

## State space models

When the likelihood integrates over a latent process, the particle filter
gives an unbiased estimate of it, and particle MCMC uses that estimate inside
an exact sampler (Andrieu et al. 2010). The latent process is written as R
functions; the static parameters and their priors come from a model.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
Tn <- 40
x <- numeric(Tn); x[1] <- rnorm(1)
for (t in 2:Tn) x[t] <- 0.8 * x[t - 1] + rnorm(1, 0, 0.5)
yobs <- x + rnorm(Tn, 0, 0.7)
ssm <- bayescomp_ssm(yobs,
  init = function(N, th) rnorm(N),
  transition = function(x, t, th) th[["phi"]] * x + rnorm(length(x), 0, th[["q"]]),
  log_obs = function(yt, x, t, th) dnorm(yt, x, 0.7, log = TRUE),
  log_init = function(x, th) dnorm(x, log = TRUE),
  log_transition = function(xn, xo, t, th) dnorm(xn, th[["phi"]] * xo, th[["q"]], log = TRUE))
pars <- bayescomp_model("
  parameters { real<lower=-1, upper=1> phi; real<lower=0> q; }
  model { phi ~ normal(0, 1); q ~ normal(0, 1); }
")
pf <- bayescomp_particle_filter(ssm, c(phi = 0.8, q = 0.5), num_particles = 300)
pf$log_lik
pm <- bayescomp_pmcmc(pars, ssm, "pmmh", num_particles = 100, chains = 2,
                      iter_warmup = 300, iter_sampling = 1000, seed = 1)
summary(pm)[, c("variable", "mean", "sd", "rhat")]
```

`method = "pgibbs"` runs particle Gibbs with ancestor sampling instead,
which needs the transition and initial densities. `pm$states` holds the
sampled latent paths.

## Large data

`bayescomp_sgmcmc()` (SGLD, SGHMC) and `bayescomp_ep()` split the
likelihood over observations. They find the observation count `N` in the
data and subset every data element with `N` entries or rows; pass `subset`
for other layouts. The prior is the model on an empty data set.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
N <- 200
X <- cbind(1, rnorm(N))
yr <- as.vector(X %*% c(1, 2) + rnorm(N))
reg <- bayescomp_model("
  data { int N; matrix[N, 2] X; vector[N] y; }
  parameters { vector[2] b; }
  model { b ~ normal(0, 10); y ~ normal(X * b, 1); }
", data = list(N = N, X = X, y = yr))
ep <- bayescomp_ep(reg, sites = 4, seed = 1)
rbind(ep = ep$mean, exact = as.vector(solve(crossprod(X) + diag(0.01, 2), crossprod(X, yr))))
sg <- bayescomp_sgmcmc(reg, "sghmc", batch_size = 20, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 200,
                       iter_sampling = 1000, seed = 1)
colMeans(bayescomp_extract(sg, "b"))
```

EP is exact here because the posterior is Gaussian. SG-MCMC has no accept
step and its draws are approximate; it pays off when the data are large.

## Latent Gaussian models

`bayescomp_inla()` integrates out a latent block by Laplace approximation
and explores the remaining hyperparameters on a grid (Rue et al. 2009).

```{r}
schools <- bayescomp_model("
  data { int J; vector[J] y; vector[J] s; }
  parameters { real mu; real<lower=0> tau; vector[J] theta; }
  model { mu ~ normal(0, 5); tau ~ normal(0, 5); theta ~ normal(mu, tau); y ~ normal(theta, s); }
", data = list(J = 8, y = c(28, 8, -3, 7, -1, 1, 18, 12), s = c(15, 10, 16, 11, 9, 11, 10, 18)))
il <- bayescomp_inla(schools, latent = c("theta", "mu"), seed = 1)
s_il <- summary(il)
s_il[s_il$variable %in% c("mu", "tau", "theta[1]"), c("variable", "mean", "sd")]
```

## Model comparison

Nested sampling estimates the evidence of one model; reversible jump MCMC
samples across several and returns posterior model probabilities.

```{r}
yy <- c(0.5, 1.2, 2, 0.8, 1.6)
mk <- function(s) bayescomp_model(sprintf("
  data { int N; vector[N] y; }
  parameters { real mu; }
  model { mu ~ normal(0, %g); y ~ normal(mu, 1); }", s), data = list(N = 5, y = yy))
ns <- bayescomp_nested(mk(2), num_live = 200, seed = 1)
c(estimate = ns$log_evidence, se = ns$log_evidence_se,
  exact = -0.5 * as.numeric(determinant(2 * pi * (diag(5) + 4))$modulus) -
    0.5 * sum(yy * solve(diag(5) + 4, yy)))
rj <- bayescomp_rjmcmc(list(narrow = mk(1), wide = mk(10)), iter_sampling = 3000, seed = 1)
rj
```

## Normalizing flows

`bayescomp_flow_vi()` pushes a Gaussian through planar flows and fits them
by maximizing the ELBO with gradients from reverse mode differentiation.
The density of the fit is exact, so Pareto k diagnoses it.

```{r}
fl <- bayescomp_flow_vi(corr, layers = 4, iter = 600, learning_rate = 0.05, seed = 1)
fl$pareto_k
```

## Simulation based inference

When the model is a simulator without a likelihood,
`bayescomp_npe()` trains a mixture density network on prior predictive
simulations and evaluates it at the observed summaries. The prior is a
model whose model block holds only the priors.

```{r}
prior <- bayescomp_model("
  parameters { real mu; real<lower=0> sigma; }
  model { mu ~ normal(0, 2); sigma ~ lognormal(0, 0.5); }
")
simulate <- function(th) {
  y <- rnorm(20, th[["mu"]], th[["sigma"]])
  c(mean(y), log(sd(y)))
}
np <- bayescomp_npe(prior, simulate, observed = c(0.8, log(1.4)), num_simulations = 1500,
                    epochs = 150, seed = 1)
s_np <- summary(np)
s_np[s_np$variable %in% c("mu", "sigma"), c("variable", "mean", "sd")]
```

The network is amortized: `np$posterior(new_summaries)` returns draws for
other data without retraining.
